items.body: For the fourth episode of our Musical Road to WOMEX, we head to a village room in southern Taiwan, where a group of Paiwan elders usually gather to sing their own folk songs. Into that room, one afternoon, walked a young metal drummer who had just moved home. Sauljaljui was back in Kapanan, her village in the Hengchun peninsula at Taiwan’s southern tip. Behind her were the university years, a nu-metal band, and a pile of rejected applications to Spring Scream, the festival every Taiwanese underground musician dreams of playing. She mentioned to an auntie that she still wanted to make music. The auntie said she knew somewhere… Old people’s music, she thought when the door opened onto a dozen elderly villagers with yueqin in their laps, the two-stringed Chinese moon lute, working through Paiwan songs she had never bothered to learn. She stayed anyway, pulled up a cajón, started holding the rhythm for them, and found they sang steadier for it. Soon she was playing every session, then performing with them, and they began treating her as one of their own grandchildren. It was only then, deep into that company, that she thought to ask one of the old women what she was actually singing about, and got back a memory from the woman’s childhood: a flower she’d spotted high on a cliff while playing hide-and-seek, too far up to pick, so she just stood and looked at it until the spring wind carried its scent down to her. She has said she felt ashamed and warmed at once. Folk music, it turned out, could be a way of singing the land itself, and she had been sitting in the room where it happened without hearing it. So she stopped keeping time for the elders and started learning from them, taking up the yueqin alongside the children of the village. Two strings, an instrument that had never belonged to her people, and somehow enough: she found her own idiom inside those constraints, folding in Austronesian rhythms gathered on tour and playing the lute as a rhythm section rather than a melodic voice. She sings mostly in Paiwan, a language spoken by fewer than 200,000 people and outlawed for years under colonial rule. And it was the elders, in the end, who put her on the Spring Scream stage her own band had never reached. That path led out of the village and a long way from it. Her self-produced 2025 album VAIVAIK, a title that means both searching and embarking in Paiwan, took Best Indigenous Language Album at Taiwan’s Golden Melody Awards, and its opening track “Dipin Kari Tang” took Best Arrangement. That one came out of a month she spent living and playing with musicians in Mauritius, and she recorded it with the Taiwu Ballads Troupe back home. She has worked for years inside Small Island Big Song too, which links Austronesian musicians across the Indo-Pacific around the ocean they hold in common. This October she brings all of it to WOMEX in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, another island a long way from Kapanan. Below, she talks about the elders who taught her to sing, about carrying a language most of her audience will not understand, and about what she hopes to find on the island itself. She also curates a playlist of the tracks that shaped her sound, exclusively for Rhythm Passport. You’re bringing music that moved from heavy metal in college to Paiwan melodies rooted in your home village. For a WOMEX audience meeting you for the first time, how would you introduce that journey and the sound it led to? When I moved back to my hometown from the city to work, I met an auntie. I told her that I wanted to start a band and make music, so she took me somewhere. When I opened the door, I was surprised to see that everyone inside was elderly. They were playing the yueqin and singing traditional songs. At that time, I was honestly a little confused, because to me, it sounded like boring “old people’s music.” But after I joined them, I started playing the cajón to accompany them. In fact, with the rhythm of the cajón, they were able to sing together more steadily and in sync. Eventually, I started performing with them and accompanying their songs. One experience that really stayed with me was when we were invited to perform at Spring Scream, one of Taiwan’s most well-known music festivals. It’s a festival that almost every Taiwanese underground band dreams of playing. My own band had applied to Spring Scream many times, but we were never selected. Yet after I returned to my hometown, it was my grandparents from the village who brought me onto that stage. I remember standing backstage and teaching one of the grandpas how to make the “rocker” hand gesture when he went on stage. But when he got up there, he got it wrong and shouted, “Local!” instead. And somehow, the audience went even crazier! (Laughs) One day, I became curious and asked one of the grandmas, “What are the lyrics you’re singing about?” She told me about something that happened when she was a child. One day, while she was playing hide-and-seek, she saw a flower growing high up on a cliff. She wanted to pick it, but it was too far away. So she just kept looking at that flower. When the spring wind came, its fragrance carried into her heart. At that moment, I felt a little ashamed, but also deeply warmed. I realized that folk music could be a way of singing the land itself. As I spent more time with these elders, they began treating me like their own granddaughter. Being around them also made me softer and more gentle as a person. When I sang these songs with them, I felt like I was finally hearing my own true voice. It was as if I had found myself. You’ve said hearing your grandmother sing, a memory of flowers and spring wind carried in the words, changed how you understood what music could do. Does that moment still shape what you want a WOMEX showcase, and a room of strangers, to feel? I hope that when people listen to my music, they can imagine the place where I grew up, the land, the environment, the people, and the culture that have nurtured me. I believe they can hear that my music comes from somewhere real. It carries a kind of life force that has grown directly from the land. You brought the yueqin into Paiwan music by learning it alongside children in your village, even though it isn’t a traditional instrument for your people. Will it be part of what you bring to the WOMEX stage, and what does it let you do that a purely traditional set-up wouldn’t? The yueqin helped me break through creatively. It only has two strings, so there are obviously limitations to what you can do with it. But because of those limitations, I started asking myself how I could express who I am within that restricted space. I began combining the unique melodies of my own culture with the rhythms of Austronesian cultures that I encountered while traveling around the world. Over time, that became my own way of playing. So the yueqin is not just an instrument for me. It has become an important part of my musical language, and it will also be one of the main instruments I use in my performances. VAIVAIK means searching, or embarking, and the album is really about your own journey back to your language and your roots. What do you want a WOMEX audience, most of whom won’t know that story, to understand about that search when they hear it at your showcase? My culture has given me confidence. It taught me to truly believe that “tradition can be invented.” When I became brave enough to respond to my culture with my own ideas, rather than simply following what already existed, I finally felt a sense of openness within myself. It made my soul want to see the world. And now, I want to share that energy with the world without holding anything back. You’ve spoken about your father criticising your Paiwan, and feeling empty after your first award because you didn’t fully understand your own lyrics. Carrying the language to a WOMEX audience who won’t understand a word of it either, does that history change how you’ll sing it? Creating music in my native language naturally comes with its own challenges, especially because we have experienced colonization and the loss of our culture and language. But those difficulties don’t make me feel defeated. Instead, they give me strength. It’s okay if the audience doesn’t understand my language. When I stand on stage, I believe they can still feel the conviction and energy that I carry. Sometimes I think about what the world would be like if there were no language barriers. I believe what would remain is energy. And I believe the energy that my culture has given me can cross those language barriers and allow people to feel that life force. Small Island Big Song connected you with musicians across island cultures of the Indo-Pacific around the shared subject of the ocean. Las Palmas de Gran Canaria is an island too, out in the Atlantic. Is there something about performing on another island, so far from your own, that you’re curious to explore there? I want to learn more about the history, people, culture, and environment of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria. I’m also looking forward to experiencing the place beyond simply being there as a performer. I want to walk through the city, meet the people, and understand how this land lives and breathes. Your records fold Mauritian rhythms and jazz and rock in next to Paiwan tradition. In a WOMEX programme full of the world’s traditions, how do you want that mix to land, and what do you hope people take from your showcase? In the past, when I created music that involved cultural fusion, it was mostly about combining different musical styles. But “Dipin Kari Tang” was different. I lived there for a month, spending every day with local people, living together and jamming together. So this song wasn’t something I imagined from a distance. It came from a real experience and became part of me. In my culture, recognition and belonging can sometimes be more important than blood relations. If we recognize one another, then we are brothers and sisters. That’s the feeling I hope “Dipin Kari Tang” can bring to people. Even if we come from different places and different cultures, if we are willing to recognize and accept one another, we can become family. You’ve said people don’t need to remember your name, only your culture. WOMEX is built around industry attention on individual artists and their catalogues. How do you hold onto that idea in a room like that? I never imagined that one day I would step outside of myself through my music. For me, I’m really just a messenger, a person who carries and shares the things I believe in. And strangely, that gives me a sense of freedom. It’s something that exists on a spiritual level. At the same time, in the commercial world, I hope I can bring these two sides together, the spirit I believe in and my identity as a musician. I am Sauljaljui. I come from the Indigenous people of Taiwan. You wear a lot of different hats, singer, songwriter, teacher, festival organiser with KAPANAN back home. Beyond WOMEX, and maybe thanks to WOMEX, what’s next for you? This year, I bought a new van, and in September I’m going to start a van tour. I’ll be traveling to different Indigenous communities, spending about a month in each one, and sharing how my culture has guided me around the world and influenced my creative journey. I’ve been inspired by many people along the way, so now I want to walk into these communities myself and share what I’ve learned and experienced. I especially hope I can bring new ideas and courage to young people in the communities, and let them know that their culture doesn’t have to be a limitation. It can actually become the strength that allows us to go out into the world. If you could write a short, personal invitation to the people of Las Palmas to come and find your showcase, what would you want them to know before they arrive? I’m Sauljaljui. Your long-lost half-sibling from another mother and another father. Come and listen to what I have to say   This October, Sauljaljui carries the songs of the Paiwan elders who taught her, and the two-stringed moon lute she learned beside them, onto the stage at WOMEX in Las Palmas     PLAYLIST: SAULJALJUJ X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Sauljaljui appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: “Cuando voy a la montaña, voy a mí“, sings Ana María Vahos on “Nuevos Horizontes”: going to the mountain is going to herself, and to a home unlike anywhere else. The mountain she names is home to Horizontes, a village of 195 people at 2,250 metres in the hills northwest of Medellín, where the houses carry their owners’ names on the front instead of street numbers. Vahos’s parents and grandparents lived there, and Sebastián Gómez Agudelo shot the video between the village and Medellín, following her through the streets and among her family. Born in San Pedro de los Milagros in 1993 and based in Medellín, Vahos writes and performs as a cantautora in a guitar-and-voice format, with the 2022 album Los Días behind her. She sings for El Búho, the recording name of Robin Perkins, who grew up in northern England, studied Latin American Studies in Glasgow, lived in Argentina and Mexico City, and started the label Shika Shika with Argentine producer Barrio Lindo in 2015. “Nuevos Horizontes” is the second single from Hogar, out 18 September on Shika Shika, an album Perkins built around field recordings of his own home life, of travel, of islands and of long evenings with friends. Hogar comes down from Latin focus, the fire in the middle of the house. The word for a home started out naming the fire it was built around. He made the record while putting down roots in France for the first time, and Vahos sings about the opposite journey: home as the place you go back to. Perkins hosts a listening party for the album on 13 September. Listen to “Nuevos Horizontes” HERE and pre-order your copy of Hogar following THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: El Búho – Nuevos Horizontes Feat. Ana María Vahos appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Synapscape, the German industrial duo of Philipp Münch and Tim Kniep, releases its new album “The Future” on 10 September 2026 through Ant-Zen. The 11-track record arrives on CD in a six-panel digipak and as a digital download. “The Future” mixes mechanical industrial resonance, glitch electronics and rhythm structures rooted in early EBM and downbeat minimalism, then pushes those elements through fractured textures and dark, atmospheric sound treatments. The tracklist runs “Moreish,” “Melting,” “Spring,” “Five Four,” “Dark Alliance,” “Disappear,” “Valley,” “Pick,” “To the Stars,” “Move” and “Work.” The Future by Synapscape The album is the duo’s first full-length since “Still” in 2018, continuing a catalog that Philipp Münch and Tim Kniep have built almost entirely on Ant-Zen, their home label since 1995. About Synapscape Synapscape formed in Bielefeld, Germany, in 1994, when Philipp Münch and Tim Kniep began working together on rhythmic-noise and industrial material. The duo debuted on Ant-Zen with its self-titled album in 1995 and followed it with “Rage” in 1997 and “So What” in 1999, records that paired heavy sequenced beats with noise and power-electronics textures. “Positive Pop” followed in 2001 and “Raw” in 2002, before “Act!” in 2005 and the collaborative “Scenes From a Galton’s Walk,” made with Asche, in 2006. The project continued through “Now” in 2007 and “Again” in 2009, then “Traits” in 2011 and “Rhythm Age” in 2015, moving its sound gradually from early EBM and power noise toward the more technoid, glitch-inflected direction it has kept since. “Still” appeared in 2018 as the duo’s most recent album before the current release. Münch, who also records as The Rorschach Garden and Mandelbrot, discussed his broader catalog in Side-Line’s Click Interview with The Rorschach Garden. “The Future” extends that three-decade run on Ant-Zen with its 10 September 2026 release.

items.body: Swedish synthpop act Split Vision release “Out Of Nowhere”, the first single from their upcoming album “BetaCity”, through Town And Towers Records. The track is an uptempo, melodic synthpop song built on analogue-style synthesizers and sequenced bass lines. “Out Of Nowhere” tells the story of someone who has spent years dealing with sorrow and uncertainty, only to be confronted unexpectedly with a declaration of love: “But suddenly, you whispered in my ear – I want you to love me.” The song marks Split Vision’s first glimpse of the musical direction for “BetaCity”, which the band describes as a natural evolution from their previous release, “Echoes of a New Spell”. Where “Echoes of a New Spell” explored the synthesizers and recording approach associated with early Depeche Mode, “BetaCity” turns toward the early sound of Alphaville, combining warm analogue synthesizers with colder digital textures, wavetable sounds and cinematic synth pads. Split Vision signed with the Scandinavian label Town And Towers Records in 2022 and has since released several singles and EPs; “BetaCity” is planned as the band’s next full-length, on CD and vinyl. About Split Vision Split Vision formed in 1985 in Sweden, when two teenage friends began writing synthpop influenced by Depeche Mode, Yazoo, Erasure and Pet Shop Boys. The line-up grew to four members through high school, and the band played discotheques in North Eastern Skåne in the late 1980s, also appearing on regional radio programmes and talent competitions. In 1988, the single “How Will I Ever” appeared on Platinum Records, followed by a minor Swedish hit with “So Many Times”. The group split up shortly after. Two of the original members, Dan Hansson and Henric Palmqvist, revived Split Vision in 2019, releasing the album “Among the Stars” on 1 October 2020, a record structured around lyrics and soundscapes referencing the cosmos. A music video for the song “Lust”, directed by Norwegian filmmaker Öystein Thorsen, followed in August 2024 and was selected at several international film festivals. Since signing to Town And Towers Records in 2022, Split Vision has released a string of singles and EPs, building toward “BetaCity”, the band’s next full-length album.

items.body: Dismantled are back with new material. Gary Zon‘s electro-industrial project will release the new single “Zero” on 18 September 2026 through Metropolis Records, with a new full-length album set to follow in November. The six-minute track is already listed by digital retailers as a Metropolis release, while the label’s current Dismantled page continues to carry the project’s catalogue. There is considerably more history behind “Zero” than the announcement might initially suggest. The track first surfaced as part of a three-song preview for an album called “Endless”, uploaded to Dismantled’s Bandcamp in November 2021 alongside previews of “Mirror’s Edge” and “Poison”. At the time, the album was expected in 2022 through Metropolis Records in North America and Dependent Records in Europe. The project itself had been announced even earlier. In May 2020, Zon revealed through Metropolis that he was working on an album titled “Endless”, which he described at the time as combining different periods of the Dismantled catalogue into a more cohesive sound, specifically referencing Standard Issue, the self-titled debut and The War Inside Me. That announcement accompanied “No Escape”, a track written during the early months of the pandemic. Six years later, a current retail listing gives “Endless” a 20 November 2026 release date on CD, with the catalogue number/EAN 0782388148320. Metropolis has not yet published a complete 2026 album page, tracklist or detailed production credits, so those details remain unconfirmed for now. “Zero” therefore functions both as the beginning of Dismantled’s new release cycle and as the return of material that has been evolving publicly for several years. The single is listed at 6:14 and will be available digitally in 24-bit/44.1 kHz resolution. Beatport currently categorises the track under Ambient / Experimental and lists it at 110 BPM, although Dismantled’s own history has always been rooted much more broadly in electro-industrial, EBM and electronic music. About Dismantled Dismantled began as a studio experiment by Gary Zon in late 2000, initially inspired by the sound of Front Line Assembly. Zon gradually added vocals and drew on influences from film, television and electronic music, developing a layered combination of electro-industrial electronics, melody and trance elements. A first demo appeared through mp3.com in 2001; Dependent Records subsequently included “Purity” on its Septic II compilation, and Metropolis Records contacted Zon later that year. The self-titled debut followed through Metropolis in 2002, with Post Nuclear arriving in 2004. Later releases included the Breed To Death EP, Standard Issue, The War Inside Me in 2011, the Whole Wide World EP in 2012 and The Hero in 2016. Metropolis currently lists “No Escape” from 2020 as Dismantled’s most recent release in its catalogue. “Zero” marks the project’s first new material in six years. For now, what is confirmed is simple: “Zero” arrives on 18 September via Metropolis Records, and a new Dismantled album follows in November. All available evidence points toward that album being the long-developed Endless, but complete official album details from Metropolis are still awaited.

items.body: British violist, singer and composer Sophie Sirota released the remix album “Pressure Drop Remixed” on 10 September 2026 through Coastal Electronauts, the Whitstable, Kent collective on which she is a co-organiser alongside Martin Glover‘s associate Peter Coyte. The ten-track set reworks Sirota’s 2025 debut “Pressure Drop” through contributions from Youth (Killing Joke bassist and producer Martin Glover, who supplies two remixes), 4hero, Coyte’s own Shape Navigator alias, 3Head/Al Mac, Will Materialise, smelliott, BorjeNotBorje, Grace Griffin Blustery Day and Riigs. The release-day single “If I Wrote A Song Would You Like It? (Shape Navigator Remix)” carries a new video edit by @diz_qo, the visual artist who works regularly with Coastal Electronauts. Of the clip, @diz_qo said: “I was seeking inspiration for it and found an old photo I’d taken years ago of what I believe to be some kind of radar equipment. It somehow resonated with the track – its sense of transmitting and receiving, of searching for a signal – and became the starting point for its visual language.” Two other tracks from the album preceded it as singles, each with its own @diz_qo video edit: Youth’s nine-minute rework of “50:50 Pure Trance”, which Side-Line covered on its own release, and “mood (4hero remix)”, whose video arrived the same month. Coyte mixed and mastered the original “Pressure Drop” album, which made his contribution to the remix set direct. Sirota commented: “Peter has given me considerable support and encouragement during my solo journey, and we have collaborated on several live projects. He also mixed and mastered the original ‘Pressure Drop’ album, so asking him to remix something from it was inevitable. The result is this beautiful track.” On the remix project as a whole, Sirota said she gave contributors free rein: “I’ve been fortunate to work with some incredible musicians during my career and it has been humbling to receive so many positive reactions to the idea of making it. What each contributor has sent back has resulted in a really eclectic variety of styles and sounds. I left each remix to their discretion and deliberately gave no direction or input.” She also pointed to newer names on the tracklist: “I’m particularly pleased to have had a number of younger artists provide unique interpretations of my tracks, including people I have met through the vibrant EMOM scene. After all, this is what gave me the initial encouragement and support to create the original album.” The full “Pressure Drop Remixed” tracklist runs: “50:50 Pure Trance – The Endless Carousel of Lust and Suffering Dub (Youth remix)”, “mood (4hero remix)”, “if i wrote a song would you like it? (Shape Navigator remix)”, “sophie’s tension (3Head/Al Mac remix)”, “i feel (Will Materialise remix)”, “holding te (smelliott remix)”, “i feel (BorjeNotBorje remix)”, “if i wrote a song would you like it? (Grace Griffin Blustery Day remix)”, “holding tension (Riigs remix)” and a second Youth reading, “50:50 Pure Ambient – The Savage Orient of the Heart Dub”. The album streams on Spotify, Apple Music and Amazon Music, and is available as a digital download on Bandcamp. Pressure Drop Remixed by Sophie Sirota About Sophie Sirota Sophie Sirota is a classically trained violist, singer and composer who began working as a session violist while at music college, going on to work as a session player, live performer, arranger and composer with Paul Weller, Kim Deal, Tindersticks, Beth Orton, Ed Harcourt, 4hero, D’Influence, Gabrielle and Robert Kirby; her Discogs profile lists close to 100 credits and a place in the Wrecking Crew Quartet. She has lived in Whitstable, Kent for more than two decades. In early 2023 she started performing solo material, built from electric viola, effects pedals and voice, at the monthly Coastal Electronauts electronic-music sessions in Whitstable, which she now helps organise. That work led to her debut album “Pressure Drop”, released on 24 October 2025 through Coastal Electronauts on digital, CD and a 100-copy vinyl edition, mixed and mastered by Peter Coyte. Record Collector called the album “a fine example of innovative artistic imagination”. “Pressure Drop Remixed”, out 10 September 2026, extends that debut into collaborative territory, opening Sirota’s viola-based material to Youth, 4hero, Coyte’s Shape Navigator project and a wider group of electronic producers. No dedicated Wikipedia page for Sirota could be found at the time of writing.

items.body: Berlin-based Dutch-Italian composer Aimée Portioli, who records as Grand River, returns to Editions Mego with her new album “Temporary”, out 20 November 2026. It is her first album for the label since 2023’s “All Above.” The lead single, “Let me know when you’re pure,” is out now on Bandcamp, Spotify and Apple Music, with the album available to pre-order on Bandcamp. “Temporary” was written after a period of personal grief and loss and centers on the interplay between resonant guitar work and electronics across eight tracks. The Bandcamp track listing runs: “18 circles to heaven,” “Come to stay,” “The crossing of the body, the crossing of the mind,” “The little we last,” “Let me know when you’re pure,” “From the other side,” “Maybe I am dead and this is paradise” and “Work of ending.” The eight titles form fragments of a longer sentence about transience, read in sequence across the record. Portioli commented on the album’s origins: “Sometimes, when travelling in places far from home that I know I will most likely never return to, or while accompanying someone I loved towards the end of their life, I become intensely aware of the singularity of the moment, and of how precious and sad this feels at the same time. It carries a particular weight because it will never happen again in quite the same way. Through experiences like these, I have gradually come to understand the temporary nature of all things. They taught me that to live is to experience the present while already feeling the trace of its disappearance, something both painful and blissful.” Temporary by Grand River Grand River live dates for ‘Temporary’ Portioli will premiere “Temporary” live at the Venice Music Biennale (Biennale Musica) before further European and Asian dates: 23 October 2026 – Biennale Musica, Venice, Italy (album premiere) 29 October 2026 – Berghain, Berlin, Germany 6 November 2026 – Mira Festival, Barcelona, Spain 7 November 2026 – Simple Things Festival, Bristol, UK 20 November 2026 – MUTEK, Tokyo, Japan Further dates have not been announced. About Grand River Grand River is the recording name of Aimée Portioli, a Dutch-Italian composer and sound designer based in Berlin. She began the project in 2014, after working as a sound engineer and composer for the Italian national radio station Radio 24 and co-founding the sound agency TapTempo studio with Luca Sammartin. Her first release, the EP “Crescente,” came out in 2017 on Spazio Disponibile, the label run by Donato Dozzy and Neel, and was named one of the year’s best EPs by XLR8R. Her debut album, “Pineapple,” followed in 2018, also on Spazio Disponibile. Portioli signed to the Vienna-based label Editions Mego for her second album, “Blink a Few Times to Clear Your Eyes,” released in September 2020. Since 2016 she has run the label One Instrument, which invites artists to record a piece using a single instrument; its catalog includes releases by Donato Dozzy and Felicity Mangan. Her third album, “All Above,” followed on Editions Mego in February 2023, dedicated to label founder Peter Rehberg, who died in 2021. In 2024 she released the collaborative album “In uno spazio immenso” with Abul Mogard on Caterina Barbieri’s label Light-Years. “Tuning the Wind,” a piece originally composed in 2022 for multichannel and 4DSOUND installations, was released as an album via Umor Rex in March 2025. Portioli has also contributed to compilations for Ghostly International and Tresor, and has performed at Berlin Atonal, CTM, MUTEK Montréal, Spain’s WOS festival, and venues including the Centre Pompidou in Paris, the Barbican in London and Berghain in Berlin. “Temporary,” out 20 November 2026 on Editions Mego, is her fourth solo studio album and the first live premiere of the record takes place at the Venice Music Biennale on 23 October 2026.

The video was filmed on location in Japan. “This video represents a watershed and introduces a new era,” TourdeForce’s Christian Ryder stated. The band plans to follow it within a month with a new single and video featuring lead singer Neviah Luneville on vocals. About TourdeForce TourdeForce is an Italian electro-wave and electro-pop project whose recent work Side-Line has followed closely. The band released the album “Vargtimmar” in December 2020, followed by two tribute singles to Death In June: “Six in the Key of Death” in January 2022 and a cover of “The Calling” with an accompanying video in March 2022, before revisiting older material on the compilation “Compendium vol. 1” that June. In April 2025, the project released a single paying tribute to the defunct EKP label. TourdeForce returned in February 2026 with the full-length album “Leaving Nothing Left Behind”, followed in March by an official video for the “LNLB” single mix. “A Good Death” is the latest video from that album, with a new single featuring vocalist Neviah Luneville expected next.

items.body: Margate, Kent-based musician Tim Horne has released “An Ocean Apart”, the first single from his new album “Transmutation”, out October 8, 2026, on Coastal Electronauts. Horne composes cinematic ambient and electronic music using synthesisers, acoustic instruments and field recordings. “An Ocean Apart” comes with a video by @diz_qo, built around artwork by Mariz Nigro, and the single is also available on Spotify and Apple Music. Horne describes “An Ocean Apart” as the emotional core of the album. “It forms the emotional core of the album and is imbued with paradoxical feelings of distance and closeness, isolation and connection. These are contradictory emotions I’ve oscillated between when looking back with unreliable memory and nostalgia,” he said. Tim Horne’s ‘Transmutation’ due October 8 “Transmutation” runs eight tracks: “Requiem,” “Halcyon,” “Biota,” “An Ocean Apart,” “Volta,” “Folie à Deux,” “Ascension” and “Metamorphosis.” Horne wrote, performed and produced every track himself, with additional mixing and mastering by Thomas Farmer and artwork by Mariz Nigro. The album was recorded towards the end of a long-term relationship and works through contradictory memories of joy and sorrow alongside an embrace of change. Horne layers flute and other acoustic instruments with analog, digital and modular synthesizers, often processing them until they no longer resemble their source material. He has pointed to Wendy Carlos, Kraftwerk, Boards of Canada, Sigur Rós, M83, Radiohead, Nils Frahm, Alessandro Cortini, R Beny, Emily Sprague, Ann Annie, Kaitlyn Aurelia Smith, Jogging House and Hainbach as influences on the record. Transmutation by Tim Horne “Transmutation” is available to pre-order now as a digital album and as a limited-edition CD in a card wallet, both through Bandcamp, with the full record following on release day. About Tim Horne Tim Horne is a musician based in Margate, Kent. He spent roughly a decade playing bass, synthesisers and backing vocals in bands including Linear Loveboxx, Inca Maps and Inigo Blue & The System before moving into solo work. He self-released two solo albums built from modular-synthesizer improvisation, “Rise” (2022) and “Clusters” (2023). Horne developed his current sound over two years through the regular live sessions hosted by Coastal Electronauts, a collective of electronic and experimental artists based in nearby Whitstable, and that process led to the eight tracks on “Transmutation.” The album, out October 8, 2026, on Coastal Electronauts, follows those two solo releases and is preceded by the single “An Ocean Apart.”

items.body: Dina Summer releases the synthpop single “Burning Heart” on 9 September 2026 via Iptamenos Discos. The track is part of the trio’s upcoming nine-track mini-album “Children Of The Night,” due 9 October 2026 on digital and vinyl. “Burning Heart” explores the pull of an imbalanced relationship, with the singer asking her partner to “cross the line” and return her affections. Sparkling organ synths sit against a propulsive dark bassline, pairing a nocturnal, club-ready sound with 1980s-style synthpop songwriting. Paris-based filmmaker Ceyda Yagiz directed the accompanying music video. “Children Of The Night” takes its title from Bela Lugosi’s line in the 1931 film “Dracula.” Iptamenos Discos will release the mini-album on black vinyl and on a blood red/black marbled vinyl edition, alongside the digital format. Dina Summer will tour behind the record, with festival dates including Wave Gotik Treffen, Amphi Festival, E-Tropolis Festival, Grauzone Festival, Out Of Line Weekender, Katzenclub Festival, Extramuralhas and Baroeg, plus headline shows in Berlin, London, Paris, Athens, Bogotá, São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Santiago and Buenos Aires. About Dina Summer Dina Summer is the Berlin-based collaborative project of Greek-German dark-disco duo Local Suicide and Bavarian electronic producer Kalipo, who began working together in 2019. The project draws on 1980s Italo disco, new wave, EBM and early-2000s electroclash for a dark, retro-futuristic synthpop sound. Dina Summer released the single “Schall & Rauch” in October 2024, then announced the mini-album “Children Of The Night” in June 2026. The trio followed with the singles “Bats in Paris” in July and “Rat Race” in August, and now “Burning Heart” arrives ahead of the mini-album’s 9 October release on Iptamenos Discos.

items.body: In 1998, a remarkable album was released as a collaborative exchange between Sonar and Muslimgauze. Eric van Wonterghem and Dirk Ivens (Sonar) created four remixes of tracks by Bryn Jones (Muslimgauze), and the process was reciprocated. However, what wasn’t known at the time was that Bryn Jones had actually produced a total of 16 remixes, leaving it up to Eric and Dirk to decide what to do with them. Following the release, performances featuring both projects were even planned, but tragedy struck when Bryn Jones passed away in early 1999. The British project Muslimgauze was extraordinary—a project I deeply admired for its sound and its unique blend of Tribal and Middle Eastern influences. Now, so many years later, these Belgian legends have decided to release the original remixes Muslimgauze created for Sonar as a standalone album, undoubtedly driven by deep respect and admiration for Bryn Jones’s masterful body of work. The result is surprising, presenting a completely transformed Sonar sound that fits seamlessly into the Muslimgauze universe. The Belgians’ signature Power-Noise is absorbed by the force of Tribal rhythms and an Eastern atmosphere, characterized by the authentic sounds of traditional instruments. Layered on top are samples of plaintive chants and voices that further enhance the mood. Muslimgauze didn’t merely create remixes; Jones undertook a complete reconstruction of the Sonar material. The overall sound is highly minimalist and perfectly embodies the Muslimgauze aesthetic. I am also struck by the brilliant stereo effects emanating from the speakers, which lend an extra touch of distinction to the production. Through this album, Muslimgauze sounds as if the project is still alive—or perhaps newly reborn. As far as I’m concerned, this is a wonderful experience. (Rating:8). Listen to “Outtake 3”: Outtake 3 by Sonar vs Muslimgauze About Sonar Sonar is the Belgian industrial and techno side-project of Dirk Ivens, also known for his work in Klinik and Dive. The project began with Ivens working alongside Patrick Stevens (Hypnoskull); Eric Van Wonterghem (Insekt, Monolith) later joined as the group’s other core member. Sonar released its self-titled debut album in 1996, followed by “Dislocated” and “On Mission Inside” in 1997. In 1998, Sonar exchanged remixes with British artist Muslimgauze (Bryn Jones, 17 June 1961 – 14 January 1999) for the collaborative album “Sonar vs Muslimgauze”, released via Prodam Records. Jones died in January 1999, shortly after the exchange was completed. “Outtakes” gathers the remaining Muslimgauze-made remixes of Sonar material that were left unused at the time.

items.body: Breaking a person rarely begins with one spectacular act. More often, it is repetition that does the work: the same insult, the same reduction, the same pressure applied until endurance is mistaken for consent. Yet endurance can hold an unexpected force of its own. A flower may bend beneath the serpent, but the serpent still depends upon the flower to keep it from falling. Los Angeles shoegaze-punk band Taleen Kali enters that struggle with “Viper,” the lead single from its forthcoming second album, AEPEX, due in early 2027 through Dum Dum Records. Written as a palindrome, the song traps aggressor and victim inside a circular design of taking, breaking, and being driven down, while its central image turns apparent fragility into an instrument of survival. “Viper” opens upon a heavy, sustained guitar figure whose shoegaze distortion carries the physical weight of metal without sacrificing melody. Taleen Kali’s voice rises through the dense guitars with a majestic, almost otherworldly radiance, pulling the song toward the grand scale of ’90s alternative rock and psychedelic shoegaze. There is also an older pop instinct beneath the volume, particularly in the way the melody keeps climbing above the riff. Around the two-minute-and-forty-five-second mark, the arrangement changes course with an almost progressive-rock turn before closing inside one final rush of guitar noise. The band explains: “‘Viper’ is written in the form of a palindrome; it has this cyclical format that isn’t like any of our previous songs. I wanted to write a song about the fractured feminine, about what can happen when we try to break someone down over and over again and again. I remember seeing this nature video of a bright blue viper coiled and perched on top of a red rose, and the rose was holding up the entire weight of this thing–it wouldn’t bend or break. It was fascinating, so it became the artwork for the single and informed a lot of the visuals of our music video.” That circular structure appears directly in the lyrics, where “Viper / Take her / Viper / Break her” reverses and repeats like a command that has become impossible to escape. Against it stands the image of the wilted flower upon an altar: burdened, objectified, and repeatedly pushed downward, yet never quite destroyed. Directed by Alex LeGolvan, the accompanying video moves between a pale woodland, an enclosed red chamber, mirrored band performances, and the physical movements of dancer Lark Detweiler. Kali appears in white beneath the trees before the imagery descends into deeper reds and magentas, where flesh, leather, metal, mirrors, and guitar strings are filmed in close detail. The dancer’s body alternately strains, recoils, and reaches outward, giving human form to the song’s repeated acts of restraint and attempted escape. The video’s viper is no metaphorical stand-in. Nagel the snake, handled by animal wrangler Lyndsey Parker, glides across the body in the final sequence, making the song’s burden intimate and tangible. Taleen Kali, Miles Marsico, Genevieve Quiquivix, and Joseph D’Alfonso appear as the band reflected in mirrors, their performance partially concealed by glass, framing, and red light. Cinematographer Kai McNight gives the forest passages a bleached, exposed quality before the enclosed scenes turn warmer and more claustrophobic. The video was edited and colored by T.J. Maries-Hunt, with guitars provided by Fender. The flower may appear delicate, but it is the structure holding the predator aloft. Watch the video for “Viper” below: AEPEX marks a darker and heavier direction for Taleen Kali, drawing upon influences including The Horrors, Sextile, L.A. Witch, Tamaryn, Curve, and Chapterhouse. Across the record, breakbeat drums, abrupt rhythmic changes, Middle Eastern melodies, massed guitar fuzz, and Kali’s movement between commanding and sugar-sweet vocals carry the band beyond the romantic punk and beach-goth character of its earlier work and into more severe psychedelic terrain. The band returned to The Cave Studios to record with engineer and producer Josiah Mazzaschi, whose credits include Light FM, Bizou, and Child Seat. Mazzaschi also mixed and mastered the album, while Chris King of Cold Showers and Kai Tak contributed additional mixing to “Aepex” and “Crossed.” AFI’s Hunter Burgan plays saxophone on the dark psychedelic riot-grrrl track “Black Rose” and bass on “Eternal Eye.” AEPEX also marks Kali’s first time serving as co-producer on a full-length album, working alongside Miles Marsico and Mazzaschi. Guitarist Genevieve Quiquivix joins Kali and Mazzaschi across the record, with former guitarist Royce Hsu contributing several cameo solos. Ciara DeAlba, Marsico, and Mazzaschi provide backing vocals. Taleen Kali released the debut EP Soul Songs in 2018, followed by the Jeff Schroeder and Josiah Mazzaschi-produced debut album Flower of Life in 2023. The band later issued the remix collection Flower of Death in 2024, and the alternative love-song covers EP Covered in 2025. Its current lineup consists of Taleen Kali on vocals and guitar, Genevieve Quiquivix on guitar, Miles Marsico on bass, and Ciara DeAlba on drums. Taleen Kali celebrates the single with a headlining performance at Bar Sinister in Los Angeles on September 12. Listen to “Viper” below and purchase the single through Bandcamp. AEPEX arrives in early 2027 via Dum Dum Records. items.body: We speak of falling in love as though gravity should handle the labor. The harder truth is that affection asks for practice: the slow unlearning of fear, vanity, possession, and the reflex to flee when another person reaches the unguarded parts of us. To say “I learn to love” is to leave the verb unfinished. It admits that tenderness is no permanent achievement, but an education measured in repetition, failure, and the willingness to try again. Austin psych-goth trio The Schisms make that unfinished education move on “I Learn To Love,” the first single from their forthcoming four-track EP, Tejas, due October 2. The song’s unruly new video was created with Austin film crew Three-Eyed Cat Collective. Led by singer, songwriter, and guitarist Carson Barker, The Schisms also feature Goose McCollum on bass, keys, and vocals and Michael Stockton on drums and vocals. The track enters on a sustained guitar figure and a firm, forward-driving beat, while Barker’s voice glides over the groove with studied ease. A blues-bitten guitar answers him in metallic clanks; the cymbals then open the ceiling as his delivery rises from a low croon into a full-throated command. Thick proto-metal chords eventually press against the rhythm section, giving the song the physical force of a taproom floor under too many boots. Much of its frame belongs to late-’60s and early-’70s rock, but an ominous synth bed disrupts the period logic midway through. A buzzing keyboard figure leans toward prog, and Barker’s voice multiplies into an eerie, reverb-drenched cascade. The old forms are dragged into an unstable present. The riff walks into the room with its collar open, while the electronics quietly change the locks. Barker wrote “I Learn To Love” as a reach toward a higher state of mind, with much of the lyric arriving spontaneously the night before the recording session. The song continued to take shape on the fly with Grammy-winning producer and engineer Stuart Sikes, known for his work with The White Stripes, Cat Power, and Loretta Lynn. Early James Brown and Bo Diddley can be heard in its insistence on rhythm, although The Schisms route that bodily drive through punk abrasion, psychedelic color, and goth unease. A mantra found a backbeat and acquired teeth; The Schisms make self-improvement sound gloriously disreputable. That productive disorder carries into the video. The clip opens on the exposed conditions of the shoot, with Stockton playing against a bare green screen as studio lights and equipment remain plainly visible. Soon the band are swallowed by liquid blue forms, clipped into circular windows, outlined like cheap television ghosts, and deposited among Texas flags, cattle, cactus country, cowboy hats, fire, leather, and collapsing VHS interference. At points, the trio look as though they were keyed into a public-access broadcast seconds before the tape began to warp. By returning to the uncovered green screen at the end, the clip makes its fakery part of its regional portrait. Texas becomes birthright and prop, affectionate cliché and private joke. Austin appears less as a civic postcard than as a fever dream assembled after last call. “For the video, we wanted to do something really trashy, like an old Captain Beafheart vid mixed with VHS-style visual effects. We also wanted something that represents Austin from a born-and-raised Texan’s point of view. There is definitely a grittier, maniacal side of Austin subcultures that often gets overlooked in the media. We wanted to pair that with cliché Texas themes. There are some throwbacks to Nathan and I’s favorite filmmakers, like Jodorowsky. The song was half-written in the studio on the fly with Stuart Sikes. It just felt like a chaotic Bo Diddley song with a dash of punk and psych, so we went with it.” Watch the video for “I Learn To Love” below: Listen to The Schisms’ “I Learn To Love” via Spotify or Apple Music, and order the single through Bandcamp. I Learn To Love by The Schisms Tejas extends the single’s upward turn. Barker wrote half of the EP during a winter spent alone in a one-bedroom log cabin in the Colorado mountains and completed the remaining material in the studio with Sikes. Isolation gave him a practical brief: write the music capable of lifting his own spirits. The result steps away from some of the darker concerns of The Schisms’ previous album, Moon, in favor of something brighter, punchier, and more open to instinct. Barker initially wrote and recorded each instrumental part before bringing the songs to McCollum and Stockton for their input. The name Tejas draws on the word’s association with friendship, while the record itself is Texas-made from end to end. Barker, McCollum, Stockton, Sikes, and Barker’s brother, who created the artwork, are all native Texans. The three musicians grew up in the same town and knew one another for years, although differences in age and timing kept them from sharing a band until the current lineup came together. “The universe just threw us together, and it’s been amazingly positive,” Barker says. His search for McCollum began with an unusually exact request: “I’m looking for a leather daddy who plays a vintage Rickenbacker bass left-handed. Know anyone?” Stockton joined after letting Barker stay at his house for a month while Barker was between homes. “The chemistry is so positive,” Barker adds, “I feel like we’re the fucking Teletubbies.” Partially funded by the City of Austin Live Music Fund, Tejas arrives October 2, 2026. Tejas tracklist: I Learn To Love One Blood All the Good Things Beyond Death The Schisms begin a 15-date fall tour on September 11 at Houston’s Black Magic Social Club. From there, the band follows the Gulf Coast to New Orleans and Jackson before moving through Birmingham, Athens, and three North Carolina stops. Nashville and Memphis carry the run into its western return through Little Rock, Dallas, Oklahoma City, and Denton. The final date brings the band home to Austin on the day Tejas is released, turning The Far Out Lounge into the record’s natural point of arrival. Tour dates: September 11 — Houston, TX @ Black Magic Social Club September 12 — New Orleans, LA @ Holy Diver September 13 — Jackson, MS @ Urban Foxes September 15 — Birmingham, AL @ The Nick September 16 — Athens, GA @ Athentic Brewing September 17 — Durham, NC @ Rubies on 5 Points September 18 — Greenville, NC @ Benny Vincenzo’s Pizza September 19 — Asheville, NC @ The One Stop September 20 — Nashville, TN @ The Cobra September 22 — Memphis, TN @ Haven Haus September 23 — Little Rock, AR @ Pizza D’s September 24 — Dallas, TX @ Craft & Growler September 25 — Oklahoma City, OK @ The Grand Royale September 26 — Denton, TX @ Anderson’s Distillery October 2 — Austin, TX @ The Far Out Lounge Follow The Schisms: Website Bandcamp SoundCloud Spotify Apple Music Instagram Facebook TikTok YouTube The post Austin Psych-Goth Trio The Schisms Unleash a Leather Clad Texas Fever Dream in the Video for “I Learn To Love” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Made your hell from the fire inside Played in flames that burned you alive What went through your head when you lost your mind The true tragedy is the world decides Something ancient in the crowd gathers around a famous death. A murder becomes spectacle; strangers study photographs, motives, wounds, and final moments as though proximity to horror might grant some secret knowledge. The macabre is easiest to enjoy when the dead are unknown to us, when grief belongs to another household and blood has no familiar name. Tragedy, then, can be consumed as theater, mystery, even entertainment. We call it curiosity, but often it is appetite dressed in respectable clothes. Civilization may depend, in part, on remembering that every spectacle was first a human life actually lived. We’ve seen it played out countless times in real life, as well as in profound films like Day of the Locust. Seattle goth dance-punk trio Holy Death Temple return with their fourth single, Nobody Loved You, a murder ballad that is shamelessly poppy and driven by a fiery bassline and fierce drumming that make the song feel almost indecently buoyant. Bryan Edward’s programming gives the track the clean immediacy of gothic synth-pop, while Jon Barrysmith’s drums keep the floor moving beneath it. Wren Rose folds guitar, synth, and backing vocals into the arrangement without crowding the hook. Edward handles lead vocals, guitar, and programming; Barrysmith (Year of the Cobra, Rifflord) takes drums; Rose (Broken Focus) supplies guitar, synth, and backing vocals. There is a little Sisters of Mercy gloom in the DNA, some Depeche Mode pop precision, and enough dance-punk velocity to place Holy Death Temple comfortably alongside ACTORS, Sextile, and VR SEX. Nobody Loved You finds its real character in the gap between what the body hears and what the lyrics are saying. The song examines the public appetite that gathers around violent death, particularly the urge to turn murder into a referendum on character. Someone dies, and almost immediately spectators begin sorting themselves into camps, prosecuting the dead, defending the killer, reconstructing motives, and deciding who deserved what. Condemnation becomes a recreational drug with excellent engagement numbers. The man at the center of the lyrics is controlling, cruel, hungry for power, and shaped by abandonment that eventually curdles into brutality. His wife endures pain and sacrifice until the arrangement ends with death. Holy Death Temple lets the listener enjoy condemning him for a while, then complicates that satisfaction by asking why everyone becomes so obsessed with determining whether a death was justified while showing far less interest in how a human being arrived at such a miserable destination. That question feels particularly sharp in an age where high-profile killings become participatory entertainment, complete with amateur detectives, moral tribunals, leaked photographs, podcast episodes, TikTok theories, and millions of strangers inspecting somebody else’s catastrophe from bed. Bryan Edward seems fully aware of how strange it is to package all of this inside something so catchy: “Never thought we’d explore our fascination with high-profile murders and repressed Erasure influence in the same song, but here we are,” he quips. “…Nobody Loved You is a mercy-killed synth-pop demo resurrected with a hook intended for a completely different track. Our best moments come from botched experiments and happy accidents.” Listen to Nobody Loved You below and order the single here. Nobody Loved You by Holy Death Temple Nobody Loved You is a bright synth-pop ‘mistake’ with a body in the trunk, built for the dance floor while staring straight at one of civilization’s uglier appetites: the thrill of death when the grief belongs to somebody else. items.body: Hands in the sky and then we die Our hearts have joined the thousand We take a step into the night Opening our eyes brings a new dawn The Goth subculture has survived for nearly half a century partly because every few years somebody remembers that death can be absurd. Strip away that humour and the genre starts resembling a homeowners’ association for people with excellent boots: approved haircuts, approved records, approved photographs taken beside approved statues in approved cemeteries. Then Comes Silence have enough mileage behind them to recognize the danger. Remaker Redeemer finds the Stockholm trio Alex Svenson, Jonas Fransson, and Hugo Zombie treating the graveyard as a playground again. Then Comes Silence fortunately remembers that a black shirt is still a shirt. The album itself is conceived as a diptych, with “Requiem” representing darkness and “Ballroom” representing light. “Everything exists in contrast,” the band says. Remaker Redeemer introduces the “Ballroom” half of the band’s forthcoming Requiem Ballroom, due November 20. The band explains that the song “is about new life, being reborn with old sins washed away. A kind of cleansing, a fresh start, and the feeling of beginning again. The choice of instruments and sounds on this track was also a way to explore something a bit different this time.” Svenson’s bass plants every movement firmly beneath the feet, while Fransson’s drums drive the song with a dark, danceable force reminiscent of Killing Joke’s Night Time era. Svenson’s grave, commanding vocals strengthen the comparison, while Zombie’s guitar cuts through with a bright, sharp edge. There is genuine pleasure in the performance, closer to liberation than solemn contemplation, which suits a song concerned with starting over. Rebirth here apparently requires amplification, eyeliner, and several people dressed as failed medical experiments. The song’s lyrics treat death as a passage toward renewal, moving from surrender and darkness toward another existence. Closed eyes, raised hands, joined hearts, and the arrival of dawn suggest a collective transformation, while the repeated call to a remaker and redeemer turns rebirth into an act of cleansing: old sins washed away, one life surrendered, and another beginning on the other side. The video makes the album’s concept pleasantly mischievous. Renewal takes place among monsters. Cleansing occurs in a room full of freaks. Life returns while death watches from the front row. Directed by Damon Zurawski of Future Legends Films, the video places the band before a congregation of ghouls, Droogs, demons, grotesques, and evil babies. Yes, evil babies that look like escapees from the bargain bin of some forbidden 1970s horror shop, which immediately gives the clip more personality than another five minutes of serious men staring into industrial fog. Zurawski photographs the performance beautifully while allowing the absurdity to breathe. Svenson holds court on bass and vocals with severe composure while Fransson hammers away behind him and Zombie sends guitar across the room in sharp strokes. Around them, the assembled creatures stare, convulse, leer, and generally behave like the clientele of a nightclub whose liquor license was issued by Satan. Watch the video for Remaker Redeemer below: Rock music periodically develops the delusion that dignity equals importance, an especially fatal mistake for any subculture born from makeup, theatrical clothing, cheap smoke machines, horror films, and teenagers trying to scandalize their parents. The original punk impulse understood spectacle as provocation. Somewhere along the road, certain corners of underground culture began treating their uniforms with the solemnity of military dress. That final joke may be the best one. Subcultures survive through mutation, bad taste, risk, exaggeration, and people willing to make fools of themselves in public. Then Comes Silence understands that preservation without mischief eventually becomes embalming. Remaker Redeemer puts the corpse back on its feet, gives it a bass guitar, and lets the evil babies dance. Then Comes Silence are currently on tour in mainland Europe. items.body: Punk may have changed the musical landscape and proved that anyone with a guitar and a mission statement could start a band, but the years that followed expanded punk’s simplicity in countless exciting directions. Sometimes, it blows my mind just how many incredible bands and movements formed in the wake of the punk explosion. From 1976-1982 alone, the sheer amount of musical creativity is staggering, with so many bands quick to combine punk’s feral, DIY essence with art rock instrumentation; spacier, dubbed-out rhythms; bleak industrial textures; and much, much more. In the UK, hundreds of bands formed in the wake of the Sex Pistols, who begat Joy Division, The Banshees, and Cabaret Voltaire, who begat thousands of other bands that we all know and love today. One of the most lasting and beloved bands from the original UK post-punk boom was Sad Lovers & Giants. Formed in Watford in 1980 by Garce (Simon) Allard, guitarist Simon Blanchard, bassist Cliff Silver, drummer Nigel Pollard, and keyboardist/saxophonist David Wood, Sad Lovers & Giants (SLAG for short), quickly signed with Last Movement and Midnight Music and released a string of crucial early singles as a statement of intent. During those early years, the band was extremely prolific, cutting two moody full-length LPs in addition to these singles, each track as powerful as the last. The band caught the ear of John Peel and cultivated a devout cult following both on the strength of their studio recordings as well as their explosive live show. Soon after, the band would splinter, with Blanchard and Pollard leaving to form The Snake Corps. In 1987, SLAG would reform with a new lineup and release three incredible records that saw the band expanding their sound and influencing the budding dream pop movement. 1987’s The Mirror Test is a landmark album for me personally, and it’s impressive to hear the album’s lush textures reflected in countless bands today. Again, in 1991, the band went on hiatus, but have since returned in the new millennium and have rekindled the spark that brought them together all those years ago. Since reuniting in 2002 (and again in 2009 with Hicks), the band has performed hundreds of gigs (including their first series of shows in North America in 2016), recorded a session for LA’s Part Time Punks, released a handful of standalone singles, and recorded two full-length LPs. Their latest release, this year’s The Weight of Forgotten Dreams, features ten new tracks, all of which stay true to SLAG’s majestic sound and atmospheric energy. The album is currently available on CD, digital, and vinyl, and will be followed up by a highly anticipated documentary that aims to capture the band’s many evolutions and highlights over their 40+ year career. We had the chance to catch up with the current incarnation of SLAG, including vocalist/guitarist Garce Allard, original drummer Nigel Pollard, and current members Tony McGuinness, Will Hicks, and Ian Gibson, about the new album, the band’s legacy, and more. Former guitarist and close friend Simon Blanchard also drops in for a spell… Congratulations on the new album! Can you tell us a bit about the recording of it? Garce: Our writing and recording processes aren’t separate. We have home studios in which we produce demos that are saved into a SLAG Dropbox, there are files for demos, instrumentals and raw vocal and sax stems. If anyone comes up with a demo it goes in the appropriate file. I always save a AIFF of my raw vocals at every stage. Usually what happens next is that the demos are played at rehearsal and everybody contributes ideas. Quite often these ideas are road tested at live shows and subtle changes are made, then it’s back to the original demo which gets an upgrade. When the demo file and instrumental file look like they are full enough to consider an album we produce a provisional running order and work out what needs doing to each track before it can be handed over to Igor and Tony to mix. Effectively, all the recording is done at home. The only time we go into a recording studio is if I need to ‘perform’ my vocals as we often notice they are different when I sing them in front of other people. This didn’t happen with the new record, so every vocal was recorded in the studio at the bottom of my garden. On a personal note, I write all the lyrics and whilst the others freely critique them I mainly use Nigel as a specific sounding board while a song develops, but Tony ultimately produces my vocals from the raw stems that I have comp’d and uploaded to the Dropbox file. Tony is the only person on the planet I would trust to edit the actual words I write as happened with a song on The Weight of Forgotten Dreams where I just got lost in thickets of words which needed a sympathetic pruning! Very occasionally we look in the demo files and there’s a long forgotten piece of music that is 95% album ready. This actually happened on this record. It’s been eight years between Mission Creep and The Weight Of Forgotten Dreams – were you working on the record all this time, or were you focused on other things? Garce: Song writing is a perpetual thing but the other project we’ve worked on over the last three years is the SLAG documentary being produced by Jean Paul Van Mierlo who did the excellent Adrian Borland film Walking in the Opposite Direction. This is with the same film maker Marc Waltman. This is your second record working with Igor Garanin – can you share some stories about working together? Garce: Igor is a mix engineer Tony knows through Above & Beyond and he did such a great job on Mission Creep that we used him again on the new album. Tony works with Igor in the studio and then sends us mixes for comment. How has your songwriting style evolved over the years? Garce: If you mean the way we get to a finished album, then the human process is very similar but the technology available now means we don’t have to do the traditional ‘recording studio’ thing. In that sense, we are effectively self-producing, whereas before, the person paying for the studio, i.e., Nick Ralph if it was Midnight Music, had a large say in the overall production decisions and the ‘style’ of the finished songs. But I think what you mean is the evolution of our style of song. Many other people will have many differing views on this and which album they like best and I accept it has changed subtly from album to album. Not a lot has changed vocally other than I’ve got better at writing melodies and perhaps more focused on saying what I want, in the way I want, in order to compliment the music and bring out the best in a song. Changes in personnel obviously bring an element of change so the key personnel swap was Tony McGuinness for Simon Blanchard on guitar after the second album. I could write an essay on that. Then there was Juliet Sainsbury (currently lives in LA) on keyboards in the eighties, she was the most accomplished keyboardist we’ve had so what she plays the others wouldn’t have been able to. Then we’ve had Cliff Silver on bass replaced by Ian Gibson and both are like chalk and cheese as musicians and songwriters. The net result of all this in my opinion, is that if anything the cinematic quality of the ambient strings and ‘wet’ noise has become more lush and expansive but…to a listener coming to the band now, the songs on the latest album have all the same sonic qualities and idiosyncrasies as all the other albums. We have a distinctive SLAG sound which we understand and respect. Nigel: Our style has not really changed over the years; we all know what makes a good SLAG song . Our songs stand the test of time, and I personally cannot distinguish between songs written 40 years ago to those that are on our latest album. Garce has and continues to write very emotional and evocative lyrics which many fans can connect with. Can you expand on some of the lyrics or themes behind the record? Garce: “We will be ashes, we will be silent and old, we will be wisdom, we will be left in the cold” were the lyrics I wrote as a twenty four year old for our second single “Things We Never Did.” I am now far older than the age I envisaged in that song and I have no intention of being silent or of being left in the cold! Broadly, I would describe my lyrics as ‘English Melancholia’ but I noticed a wry-ness creeping in over the course of this recent album, although given that I am writing about the state of the world as I currently see it there’s precious little to chuckle about; call it gallows humour. As a device, I often write against a fictional dystopian backdrop (“Asylum Town,” “Repentance Day,” “Down To The Wire”), but increasingly the dystopia has become reality since the last album in 2018. Unfortunately, that does seem to be the case, doesn’t it? Sad to think that all the prophecies, whether it be in lyrics or films or literature has come true, in a sense. On a lighter, but related note, what else, other than music, do you tend to draw inspiration from? Garce: Literature and Art Nigel: Differing cultures and the great outdoors. Sad Lovers & Giants have always had such iconic artwork across both your singles and LPs. The covers alone really convey such a strong sense of emotion and perfectly reflect the music in my opinion. I’d love to hear more about what inspires your album artwork. Garce: Simon Blanchard designed the sleeves for the first three singles, including the image for “Lost In a Moment” (girl in armchair with teddy bear!), which is one that is particularly well known. Given that he also wrote much of the songs I think his design choices were intuitively in alignment with his songwriting. Midnight Music did the design work for many subsequent releases but they were building on the foundations he had laid. We asked Simon to design The Weight of Forgotten Dreams as he did such a great job with the previous album, Mission Creep and Cherry Red Records asked him to design the box set they released. Simon: Well it’s imortant to remember I can’t claim credit for all the band’s sleevework and Tony’s contribution is not to be underestimated. It’s not always easy to provide a visual foil for their music, but having been there since the beginning, I probably have a basic understanding of the strange world they inhabit. There’s usually a lot of trial and error and this time it was helpful to have access to some of Garce’s original paintings, which I montaged-up with the photography. To me it felt that the result sat well with the music and luckily the band liked it. Will you be touring for this record? Garce: In SLAG world there are three things happening currently. The Weight Of Forgotten Dreams, the film and then the live double album recorded for the film, so we will be playing live more over the next two years to coincide with this creative phase. I was happy to hear that the band finally came to the US after all these years, but sadly I live in New York and couldn’t make it to the West Coast/Austin shows. Do you plan to come back to North America at all? Garce: We want to come back and at some point over this next two years would be great timing but we are not in any specific discussions at present. Obviously as we did the West Coast plus Canada and SXSW in Austin last time, the East Coast and New York would be a priority next time. In the Breeze-era lineup. Photo by Cliff Ash. Looking back to the formation of the band, can you tell us a bit about how you all came together? Garce: The band was originally formed by Simon, Nigel and Dave Wood, who were at school together. They were called The Traumatics and they recruited an outside bass player called Steve Carter who sadly died quite recently. Dave played tenor sax and both Simon and Steve sang. At that time I was playing guitar (and singing backing vocals) in another local band called Suspect Device and we knew each other from playing together supporting a well known local band called Mr E and The Imaginations. Mr E had supported The Ruts at The Marquee club and the guitarist and singer of The Ruts were at our gig. I knew Dave Wood from drinking and playing pool together at The Feathers in Rickmansworth and he invited me to audition as the singer of The Traumatics. From that first meeting we knew it would work because we shared the same musical tastes. Our first London gigs were performed as The Traumatics with Steve Carter on bass. When we did “50:50” he sang it and I played keyboards. We changed the name from The Traumatics to Sad Lovers & Giants in January 1981. Sometime after the first single we brought in Cliff Silver on bass who we knew from playing with other Watford bands that he was in. We also bought a string synth and Simon began experimenting with spacial guitar sounds. Dave began playing the string synth more than the sax. Simon: We formed pretty soon after the punk explosion in the late seventies. We had been listening to rock music for years before that as young teenagers but it suddenly became very clear that you could be in a band with only very rudimentary music skills. We slowly got better – but not that much. The Traumatics. Photo credit unknown. Mid-80s lineup. Photo by Nick Ralph. Was there a coherent scene in Watford? Garce: There were a lot of young bands who all knew each other and played and drank in the same pubs. There was the Watford Pub Rock competition run by the owner of the local music shop and there were several fanzines. Apart from ‘our sort of music’ i.e. Post Punk/New Wave/Alternative/Art School bands, there were other more mainstream rock and blues bands mainly comprised of older musicians. Watford was a seething mass of music and musicians but probably no different to many large towns in the early eighties. The UK music scene at that time was quite remarkable looking back on it. I listened to a BBC radio 4 programme the other day whose basic premise was that the counterculture of the ’60s didn’t die out but was boosted by punk and morphed into the indie scene of the ’80s. But then the establishment pushed back, Thatcherism (Margaret Thatcher, prime minister 1979 to 1990) was in effect a counter-counterculture where alternative views were discouraged. On the whole we weren’t overtly political but if you were in one of those young bands then you knew who the enemy was and just doing it was resistance of sorts. That was the true source of the apparent coherence. A disparate collection of bands from Watford and nearby towns got together and put out an album called The Thing From The Crypt but the DIY record scene was just a reflex in the instinctive resistance to the establishment. I love that compilation and was very happy to pick up the Dark Entries reissue a few years back! Otherwise, the band has such an iconic catalog of tracks, including bangers like “50:50,” “Seven Kinds of Sin,” “In Flux,” “Colourless Dream,” etc. that are still heard in clubs today. How do you feel about the band’s legacy thus far? Garce: When we started we were defining our sound and every new song we wrote was a step into the unknown. When we reformed in 2009 we were coming off the back of a reputation built over thirty years and eight albums so from then on there was a pressure to maintain the standards we had set. As a live band we’ve surpassed those early standards which comes not only from experience but from having a huge back catalogue of great songs to choose from; we have the songs and we know how to use them. These days we’ve scaled our live show up for some seriously large gigs and have sold out 1200 capacity venues in our own name but we are still a cult band albeit with a huge worldwide following. Sometimes I dream about suddenly becoming a mainstream act but in reality I’m quite happy being where we are. Which begs the question, “if it’s not about world domination what is it about?” Answer: the music, the fans, the international travel, the ‘pinch yourself’ moments when we achieve something surprising like having “Colourless Dream” used in the Netflix Andy Warhol series. But above all it’s about the shared experience of doing it all with your mates and…still being able to make music. As a post punk-eighties band, we are always going to be remembered for those first two albums but there are eight others and Spotify has helped get them heard with around 150,000 plays a month. I’m very proud of all of them; they are all unique and have their own story to tell. The trick with the last two has been to keep our essential ‘sound’ whilst conforming to modern production expectations because fans listen to the work recorded in the analogue world of the early eighties and the production standards of that era were completely different, nevertheless they are synonymous with what the fans think of as SLAG. That is acceptable when it’s tinged with nostalgia but not in the modern world. If I remember correctly there was hardly any compression used on the early albums, can you believe that? So I think The Weight of Forgotten Dreams sits well in the legacy scheme of things. But what next? Do we write one last happy album? Hopefully there will be many more to come! Can you share some personal highlights from over the years? Garce: Showcasing at SXSW in 2016 Nigel: Playing our first gig as Sad Lovers & Giants in our hometown of Rickmansworth, recording our second single (“Colourless Dream”) in Surrey Sound where Siouxsie and the Banshees had been recording their LP Juju. More recently playing to 5,000 people at the 2024 Visor fest in Murcia, Spain, with the Sun going down – Magical! Tony: Highlight for me was selling out Echoplex in LA at the end of our first US tour. Ian: I enjoy playing live so my personal highlights are: The first time we played The Marquee in Wardour Street – I felt it was a proper rock venue that I’d previously been to as a punter, it felt a bit surreal to me to be up on that stage in front of paying punters. Another surreal moment was my overseas debut at Club Isla near Valencia, which felt like an enormous gig to me. The Echoplex in LA was special. The festival in Murcia was too….so many great gigs. SLAG at the Echoplex in 2016. Photo by Terry Howick. Will: Playing live is definitely my favourite part of being in Sad Lovers & Giants. I love meeting the fans and other bands that we play with, I love seeing places around the world from a perspective that I wouldn’t be able to access without the network of promoters and friends that the band cultivates. I love feeling the connection with our audience during a performance – which feels like a celebration of the band, every time, and I feel privileged to be part of it and to help contribute to the legacy. In particular, I will always remember our US tour – which was a huge undertaking for the band – a chaotic yet rewarding experience of massive drives, downtown motels and passionate crowds. What’s next for the band? Garce: We play two gigs in Italy this October, then we put the final touches to the film for the rest of this year. The live album will be pressed and ready for release around then but the exact timing of everything depends on the film. Then we have a gig on a boat in Paris in March followed hopefully by a small tour of Portugal and Spain. After that there will inevitably be a series of gigs in all the usual places, namely Holland, Germany and Greece. Meanwhile the demo file will begin filling up again! § Sad Lovers & Giants’ new album The Weight of Forgotten Dreams is out now! Listen via Spotify and order here. Follow Sad Lovers & Giants Linktree Website Instagram Facebook Spotify Documentary Kickstarter Header photo by Simon Blanchard The post Down To The Wire — An Interview With Sad Lovers & Giants appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
